q: For a normal human eye, the least distance of distinct vision is taken as about:
x: The near point of a normal eye is taken as d = 25 cm, the closest distance at which an object is seen clearly without strain. 100 cm is sometimes confused with the 1 m used to define the dioptre.

q: The magnifying power of an optical instrument is defined as the ratio of:
o: the height of the image to the height of the object
the focal length of the lens to the least distance of distinct vision
the image distance to the object distance
the angle subtended at the eye by the image to the angle subtended by the object seen directly by the unaided eye
x: Magnifying (angular) power M = β/α, where β is the angle subtended by the image through the instrument and α by the object seen by the unaided eye (at the near point for a microscope). The height ratio is linear magnification, the most tempting slip.

q: A convex lens of focal length 5 cm is used as a simple microscope, with the final image formed at the near point (d = 25 cm). Its magnifying power is:
x: With the image at the near point, M = 1 + d/f = 1 + 25/5 = 6. Forgetting the 1 gives 5, the formula for the image at infinity.

q: A magnifying glass of focal length 2.5 cm is used by a person with near point 25 cm who views the final image at infinity (relaxed eye). The magnifying power is:
x: For a relaxed eye the object sits at the focus and M = d/f = 25/2.5 = 10. Adding 1 gives 11, which is the value for the image at the near point.

q: A convex lens of power +10 D is used as a magnifier with the final image at the near point, 25 cm from the eye. Its magnifying power is:
x: f = 1/P = 1/10 m = 10 cm, so M = 1 + d/f = 1 + 25/10 = 3.5. Using M = d/f gives 2.5; using P directly as 1 + P gives 11.

q: A telescope objective has a diameter of 6.1 cm and is used with light of wavelength 500 nm. By Rayleigh's criterion for a circular aperture (α = 1.22 λ/D), the smallest angle between two stars it can just resolve is about:
x: α = 1.22 λ/D = 1.22 × 5 × 10⁻⁷ / 0.061 = 6.1 × 10⁻⁷ / 6.1 × 10⁻² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ rad. Dropping the 1.22 gives 8.2 × 10⁻⁶ rad; leaving D in cm gives 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ rad.

q: Which change improves the resolving power of an astronomical telescope?
o: Using an eyepiece of shorter focal length
Covering part of the objective to reduce its aperture
Using an objective of larger diameter
x: The minimum resolvable angle is α = 1.22 λ/D, so a larger aperture D (or shorter λ) makes α smaller and resolution better. A shorter-focal-length eyepiece raises magnification, not resolution, which is the tempting confusion.

q: For a telescope, the diameter of the objective is doubled and the wavelength of light used is halved. The minimum angle of resolution becomes:
x: α = 1.22 λ/D ∝ λ/D, so α becomes (½)/(2) = ¼ of the original. Resolving power (1/α) becomes four times; mixing the two up gives the 'four times' option.

q: Magnifying power of an optical instrument has the unit:
x: M = β/α is a ratio of two angles, so it is a pure number with no unit. The dioptre is the unit of lens power, not of magnifying power.

q: A convex lens of focal length 10 cm is used as a magnifier. The virtual, erect image is formed 25 cm from the lens on the same side as the object. How far from the lens is the object?
x: Lens formula with a virtual image (q = −25 cm, real-is-positive): 1/p = 1/10 + 1/25 = 7/50, so p = 50/7 ≈ 7.1 cm. Check: M = q/p = 25/(50/7) = 3.5 = 1 + 25/10. Treating the image as real gives 1/p = 1/10 − 1/25, p ≈ 16.7 cm.

q: An astronomical telescope in normal adjustment has an objective of focal length 120 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 4 cm. Its magnifying power is:
x: In normal adjustment M = fₒ/fₑ = 120/4 = 30. Adding the focal lengths (124) gives the length of the telescope, not its magnifying power.

q: The eyepiece of an astronomical telescope in normal adjustment is replaced by one of half the focal length, with the same objective. The magnifying power:
x: M = fₒ/fₑ, so halving fₑ doubles M. Thinking M is proportional to fₑ gives 'halves'.

q: To obtain a large magnifying power, an astronomical telescope should have:
o: an objective of long focal length and an eyepiece of short focal length
an objective of short focal length and an eyepiece of long focal length
both lenses of short focal length
both lenses of equal focal length
x: M = fₒ/fₑ is large when fₒ is large and fₑ is small. Short focal lengths for both lenses is the rule for a compound microscope, the tempting mix-up.

q: In a compound microscope the objective produces a linear magnification of 8. The eyepiece has focal length 5 cm and the final image is at the near point (d = 25 cm). The magnifying power of the microscope is:
x: Total M = mₒ × Mₑ = 8 × (1 + 25/5) = 8 × 6 = 48. Using Mₑ = d/fₑ = 5 gives 40; adding instead of multiplying gives 13 or 14.

q: In a compound microscope an object is placed 1.2 cm from an objective of focal length 1 cm. The eyepiece has focal length 2.5 cm and the final image is at the near point (25 cm). The magnifying power is:
x: Objective: 1/q = 1/1 − 1/1.2 = 1/6, so q = 6 cm and mₒ = q/p = 6/1.2 = 5. Eyepiece: Mₑ = 1 + 25/2.5 = 11, so M = 5 × 11 = 55. Using Mₑ = d/fₑ = 10 gives 50; adding gives 16.

q: The image formed by the objective of a compound microscope is:
x: The object lies just outside the focal point of the objective, so it forms a real, inverted, magnified image, which the eyepiece then magnifies. 'Virtual, erect and magnified' describes the eyepiece's own action.

q: Compared with the distant object, the final image seen through an astronomical telescope in normal adjustment is:
x: The objective forms a real, inverted image at its focus; the eyepiece, acting as a magnifier, gives a virtual image at infinity that stays inverted. Real and inverted describes only the intermediate image.

q: In a spectrometer, the slit is placed at the focal point of the collimator lens so that:
o: the light converges to a point on the prism
the light leaving the collimator diverges widely
the image of the slit is formed on the turntable
the light leaving the collimator is a parallel beam
x: Light from a source at the focus of a convex lens emerges parallel, so the collimator sends a parallel beam onto the prism or grating on the turntable. The telescope then focuses the parallel beam to form the slit image.

q: An astronomical telescope in normal adjustment has a magnifying power of 20 and its two lenses are 105 cm apart. The focal length of the objective is:
x: fₒ + fₑ = 105 cm and fₒ = 20fₑ, so 21fₑ = 105, fₑ = 5 cm and fₒ = 100 cm. Taking the separation as fₒ − fₑ gives about 110.5 cm; 5 cm is the eyepiece.

q: The objective of an astronomical telescope is made with a large diameter mainly in order to:
o: collect more light and resolve finer detail
reduce the length of the telescope
x: A wider objective gathers more light (brighter images of faint objects) and lowers the minimum resolvable angle 1.22 λ/D. Magnifying power depends on fₒ/fₑ, not on the diameter, which is the common slip.

q: The Moon subtends an angle of 0.5° at the naked eye. Viewed through an astronomical telescope of magnifying power 20 in normal adjustment, the final image subtends about:
x: M = β/α, so β = Mα = 20 × 0.5° = 10°. Dividing instead of multiplying gives 0.025°; adding gives 20.5°.

q: A compound microscope has an objective of focal length 2 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. An object is 2.2 cm from the objective and the final image is at infinity. The distance between the two lenses is:
x: Objective: 1/q = 1/2 − 1/2.2 = 1/22, so q = 22 cm. For a final image at infinity this image lies at the focus of the eyepiece, so the separation is 22 + 5 = 27 cm. Forgetting fₑ gives 22 cm; adding fₒ instead gives 24 cm.

q: In Michelson's method an eight-sided mirror rotates at 600 rev s⁻¹ and the distant mirror is 31.25 km away. The light is seen steadily when the mirror turns one-eighth of a revolution during the round trip. The speed of light found is:
x: Round-trip time 2d/c equals 1/(8f), so c = 16fd = 16 × 600 × 31 250 = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Forgetting the factor 2 for the round trip gives 1.5 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; leaving d in km gives 3.0 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.

q: In Michelson's experiment an octagonal mirror rotating at 500 rev s⁻¹ turns through one-eighth of a revolution while the light makes its round trip. The time of the round trip is:
x: One revolution takes 1/500 s = 2.0 × 10⁻³ s, so one-eighth takes 2.0 × 10⁻³/8 = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ s. Taking a full revolution gives 2.0 × 10⁻³ s.

q: An optical fibre guides light along its length by:
x: Light striking the core–cladding boundary at more than the critical angle is totally internally reflected again and again, so it stays inside the core. Refraction alone would let light leak out of the fibre.

q: For light to be trapped in the core of an optical fibre, which condition must hold?
o: The core has a higher refractive index than the cladding, and light meets the boundary at more than the critical angle
The core has a lower refractive index than the cladding, and light meets the boundary at more than the critical angle
The core has a higher refractive index than the cladding, and light meets the boundary at less than the critical angle
The core and cladding have equal refractive indices
x: Total internal reflection needs light going from the denser (higher n) core towards the less dense cladding, at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle. Reversing the index order is the usual slip.

q: A glass rod of refractive index √2 is surrounded by air. The critical angle for light inside the rod is:
x: sin C = 1/n = 1/√2, so C = 45°. Using n = 2 by mistake gives sin C = ½ and C = 30°.

q: A light pulse travels along 4 km of optical fibre whose core has refractive index 1.5 (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹). Ignoring the zig-zag path, the time taken is:
x: v = c/n = 2 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, so t = 4000/(2 × 10⁸) = 2 × 10⁻⁵ s = 20 μs. Using c instead of v gives 13.3 μs; multiplying c by n gives 8.9 μs.

q: A graded-index multimode fibre spreads a light pulse less than a step-index multimode fibre because:
o: the core is so narrow that only one ray path is possible
the cladding absorbs the rays that travel at large angles
its core has a higher refractive index near the outside, slowing the outer rays
rays on longer paths travel through outer regions of lower refractive index, where they move faster
x: In a graded-index core n falls from the axis outwards, so rays that wander farther from the axis travel faster and arrive almost together with the axial ray, reducing pulse spreading. A single possible path describes a monomode fibre, not a graded-index one.

q: A monomode (single-mode) step-index fibre has a core that is:
o: wide, with a refractive index that decreases from the axis outwards
of lower refractive index than its cladding
made of a metal that reflects light
very narrow, a few micrometres across, so light travels almost straight along the axis
x: A monomode fibre has a very thin core (about 5 μm) so light effectively follows only one path along the axis. An index falling from the axis outwards describes a graded-index fibre.
